en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ji. Notes on the Verses of Faith and Understanding at the End of the Sūtra:
“At that time, Mahākāśyapa arrived; he attained it without seeking. Commentary:

While the prose section records that all four individuals received the teaching, the fact that Kāśyapa alone receives it in the verse portion is because he is the eldest in seniority and represents the intention of the entire assembly.
Therefore, the shadow [of this meaning] is manifested because others also express it in verse.
Below there are eighty-six and a half verses, divided into two parts:
the first seventy-three and a half verses comment upon the preceding three passages;
"Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One," and the following thirteen stanzas belong to the third section of this chapter, which concerns the profound depth of the Buddha's benevolence.
This section consists of three parts:

the first two stanzas praise the teaching by way of Dharma; the next forty-one stanzas praise the teaching by way of parable; and the final thirty and a half stanzas praise the teaching by way of synthesis.
This is the first [section].
It does not praise what was not sought in the past, but praises only what has been obtained in the present.
The first one and a half verses praise two matters—listening to the Dharma and listening to the record; the latter half-verse praises the attainment.
The Sūtra says: "For example, it is like a young child who is immature and lacks discernment.
The Commentary states:
The following second section consists of forty-one verses that explain the teaching through parables.
The middle section is divided into two parts:
the first thirteen and four verses (seventeen in total) praise what was not previously hoped for, while the latter seven verses praise what has now been obtained.
Within the first part, there are six sub-sections:

The first half-verse is a metaphor for the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); the next verse is a metaphor for the retrogression into the flow of birth and death; the next seven verses are metaphors for returning to see the Buddha; the next fourteen verses are metaphors for being unwilling to cultivate the Great Vehicle; the next nine and a half verses are metaphors for converting [beings] by means of the Two Vehicles; and the final two verses are metaphors for demonstrating the Great Vehicle while lacking aspiration for it.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the Sūtra passage, "He abandoned his father and fled, until more than fifty years had passed," the commentary says:
The second is the analogy of retreating and flowing through birth and death.
"Wandering throughout" (*zhōuliú*) means experiencing or traversing.
"Various lands" refers to the five destinies (*pañcagati*); collectively, they are termed "foreign lands."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, "His father, filled with anxious concern, traveled until he reached a certain city where he stayed," the commentary states:
This concludes the third section; among the seven verses that follow, there is the metaphor of once again seeing the Buddha.
The prose version has three parts:
the son’s growth and return to his country, the father’s prior search for him, and the son’s arrival at the city.
Here, however, there is only a verse on the father’s prior search for the son; the other two parts are not versified.
The two passages are placed within the fourth section of the latter part because they fit the context smoothly.
This section contains four parts:

one verse on seeking a son and leaving the city; one and a half verses on the great abundance of wealth and property; one verse on the vastness of guest profits; and one and a half verses on the many people coming and going.
This is the first point.
"Seeking in the four directions" means seeking [the child] by entering into the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
"Exhausted" refers to toil and labor; it indicates the manifestation of signs in order to seek the son.
“Dun” (頓) means to halt; he halted at the great city.
The sutra says: “He constructed houses and dwellings until the population became vast.
The commentary states:
Second, the material resources are exceedingly abundant.
"Building a house" (*zhào*) signifies the arousal of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), while "erecting a dwelling" (*lì shè*) reveals the ultimate truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Alternatively, "building" (*zhào*) means to arise; the "house" (*zhái*) is the same as the "dwelling" (*shè*, *śālā*), which refers to the mind of compassion.
The "five desires" refer to the five kinds of pleasure, or alternatively, to the five dharmas such as the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Entertainment" (*yu*) means joy.
"Carriage" (*lian*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which the Dharma King alone mounts.
"Carriage" refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), for it is ridden together by all people, yet they differ in terms of superiority and inferiority.
"Vehicles" refers to the five vehicles (pañca-yāna); "fields and estates" refers to wisdom and abandonment (jñāna-prahāṇa). The remaining text may be understood accordingly.
The Sūtra says: "The profits from its lending and borrowing reach everywhere.
The commentary states:
The three types of incidental profit are abundant and extensive.
"Shāng" (商) refers to trade; those who circulate rare and exotic goods from the four quarters are called shāng, while those who sit and sell them are called jiǎ (賈).
"Gù" (估) refers to market taxes.
Those who travel are called shāng, and those who sit are called jiǎ; the term "guest" (kè) applies generally to both.

To come and go through the six realms of existence to benefit all living beings is called "trading" (shāng); to dwell in the Pure Land, among humans, or in the heavens to transform sentient beings is called "merchandising" (jià);
to traverse the marketplace of the three realms and collect its taxes and profits is called "appraising" (gù).
Because its benefits extend widely to all, the Buddha-dharma exists throughout the three realms.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, “Countless millions of billions of beings... possessing great power and majesty,” the commentary states:
Regarding "the many who come and go":
"Many kings" refers to the fact that benevolent kings cherish him out of reverence, and noble clans, ministers, and commoners honor him.
Due to these causes and conditions, those from the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings come and go in great numbers.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "But as one grows old and decrepit, what shall one do?",
the commentary states:
The fourth section below contains fourteen verses concerning the refusal to cultivate the Mahāyāna.
There are four parts:

the first two verses describe the father constantly thinking of his son; the next nine verses describe the son seeing him and fleeing in alarm; the next one and a half verses describe the father ordering him to seize him quickly; and the final one and a half verses describe the son’s resulting distress and fear.
This is the first [section].
As his years advanced, his mindfulness increased; as the Way was long practiced, his compassion grew deep. Day and night he contemplated only the sixfold observation.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the impoverished son... or he obtained nothing at all."
The commentary states:
The second section consists of nine verses concerning the sons seeing [the lion] and fleeing in terror;
within this, there are three parts.

The first three verses describe encountering the father’s house; the next two and a half verses describe the appearance of the father as seen; and the final three and a half verses describe fleeing in alarm upon seeing him.
Within the first section, there are two parts:
the first one and a half verses concern the wandering search, and the latter one and a half verses concern arriving exhausted.
This is the first [character].
"Suo" (索) has two pronunciations: Suo Ji (所戟) and Su Ge (蘇各). It means to beg, and also to seek.
The meaning of "state" (guó) and "city" (yì) has already been explained in the long prose section.
"Having something to attain" refers to encountering a true spiritual friend within the Buddha-dharma.
"Having nothing to attain" refers to a false or superficial acquaintance.
This corresponds to the passage in the sutra where [the son], emaciated by hunger and weakness, eventually arrives at his father’s house.
The commentary says:
This is the state of being "in distress.
Because the Dharma-food is insufficient, one suffers from hunger; because wondrous practice is not perfected, one suffers from exhaustion.

If one gives rise to evil views, because they damage what is profound, sores are produced; if one fails to uphold the precepts with steadfastness, because they damage what is shallow, ringworm is produced.
Thus, one falsely generates interpretations and fails to single-mindedly maintain the precepts.
"Reaching the father's city" means encountering entry into the Mahāyāna.
"Hiring oneself out" refers to laboring for wages.
"Successively passing through" means striving diligently to seek the Dharma.
"Arriving at his father's house" refers to entering the Middle Way Mahāyāna.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra: "At that time, the elder went to the place where the deed and the promissory note were kept," the commentary says:
The second is the aspect of the father as he is perceived.
Regarding "within the gate": in principle, one dwells within the teaching; the fruit resides within the cause.
Previously, looking toward birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one was said to dwell outside the gate; now, looking toward *nirvāṇa*, one therefore dwells within the gate.
"Calculating gold and so forth" refers to the various sages composing treatises to analyze and evaluate the noble wealth of the Dharma.
"Managing assets and expenditures" refers to the practice of the two types of utility.
Regarding the term "Commentary on the Notes" (Zhujiquanshu): it refers to the commentaries composed by various masters and the textual notes they have edited and written.
"Zhu" (注) is pronounced as *ding* (dīng) with the second tone; it means to record or annotate.
The *Qieyun* states: "Zhù (注), with the phonetic transcription zhī-shù-fǎn; it means a stream of water, not a written commentary.
The *Guangya* states: "Zhù (注), also with the phonetic transcription zhī-yù-fǎn; it means a commentary (*zhùshū*), as well as to recognize and to explain."
The *Tongsu wen* states: "To record things is called 'zhù' (annotation).
Today, it is likewise written as "zhù.
In the Sūtra, [the passage] from "The impoverished son saw his father" up to "For what reason have you come here? [is cited].
The commentary states:
The three views have already fled.
This is divided into two parts:
The first one and a half verses express regret for having come; the next two verses concern his retreat.
This is the first part.
The Sūtra says: "He covered [his tracks] and thought to himself... until he wished to go out to seek work."
The commentary says:
"To turn back and flee" means to retreat.
"Pressing and urgent" means to be constrained and distressed.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the elder went to seize and bring him back.
The Commentary states:
This is the third instance where the father ordered him to be seized urgently.
"To silently comprehend" means that one has never publicly declared before the assembly that a śrāvaka encountered him in the past and is his son; this is called "silently comprehending."
The Sūtra says: "The impoverished son was startled and cried out, 'How have I come to this place!
The commentary states:
The fourth son thus became filled with anxiety and alarm.
To retreat from the Great Vehicle and fail to practice, remaining instead within the cycle of birth and death, is called "falling prostrate in stupor.
To engage in great practices that deviate from one's original intent, being no different from death itself, is called "certainly to be killed."
"What use is this Great Vehicle, with its untainted food and clothing, having suddenly come to this?
Regarding the passage from the *Sūtra* which says, "The elder knew that his son had arrived but lacked majesty and virtue," the commentary states:
The fifth section below consists of nine and a half verses that employ metaphors of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The prose commentary contains six sections, of which there are four here; the first two are not versified.

The first three verses cause one to cultivate the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); the next verse concerns the son’s subsequent reliance on practice; the following four and a half verses exhort entry into the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); and the final verse establishes the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
The first part further divides into two:
the first two verses concern the dispatching of a messenger, while the final verse concerns the delivery of the message.
This is the former.
"Foolishness" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Narrow-mindedness" refers to a limited intellect.
"Being one-eyed" refers to distorted vision.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A single eye signifies deficiency.
When the eye sockets are sunken and constricted, it is called *miao*; *miao* means small.

To preach the teachings on the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) for the sake of those of the two vehicles is to be able to express them verbally while the meaning remains incomplete; this is termed "having a sunken eye" (*miaomu*).
The principle of the emptiness of persons that it expresses is shallow; therefore, it is called "stunted" (*kua*).
It lacks the merits of the *dharmakāya* and is thus ugly; therefore, it is called "ugly" (*lou*).
Its spiritual function is not extensive; therefore, it is called "lacking majesty and virtue" (*wu weide*).
The Sūtra says: "You may say to him... up to 'I shall give you double the price.
The Commentary states:
This is the transmission of the message.
Regarding the sutra passage from “The impoverished son heard this” up to “he entered the clean rooms,” the commentary states:
The two sons then proceeded accordingly.
"Clearing away the filth of afflictions and purifying the house of the five aggregates.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, "The elder, at the window, considers worldly pleasures to be base matters," the commentary says:
The three verses and a half on "Exhorting Entry into the Roots of Goodness" consist of three parts in the prose commentary, and these likewise have three parts:
the first verse expresses grief of heart; the second verse concerns physical proximity; and the latter two and a half verses concern conversing together.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sūtra passage, “Thereupon the elder went to where his son was,” the commentary says:
This refers to being close at hand.
The Sūtra states: "Through skillful means, he draws near until he is as if my own son.
The commentary says:
Next is the section on conversing.
The prose portion has two parts, and this section likewise has two:
the first half-verse provides a general exhortation to converse, while the subsequent two verses provide specific instructions through discourse.
The subsequent text consists of two parts:
the first one and a half verses grant [the teaching] immediately upon request, while the latter half of the verse feigns a father-son relationship.

Regarding "oil for anointing the feet": among the common people in the West, it is customary to go barefoot; since the weather is often warm and dusty, they invariably wash their feet and apply oil to them whenever they return home.
What is now called the "feet" refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*):
desire, diligence, mind, and investigation.
"Oil" refers to the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), namely: desire, diligence, faith, pliancy, right mindfulness, right awareness, volition, and equanimity.

The first three [limbs] constitute the preparatory stage (*prayoga*): pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) sustains the body and mind; right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right situational awareness (*samyak-samprajanya*) serve as its adjuncts, because they prevent forgetting the object of focus and settle the mind in a single state.

Because one understands as it truly is that negligence gives rise [to these states], volition (*cetanā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) serve as their antidotes through the two powers of uplifting the mind and stabilizing the mind.

Thus, one is able to distance oneself from sinking and agitation once they have arisen; this is called "anointing the feet with oil," which is like removing wind-stiffness, for it severs the obscurations of defilement.

Alternatively, the feet may be said to represent the precepts, and the oil represents the six branches. Having received and trained in the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), one is well able to guard the Prātimokṣa restraint; one’s conduct and deportment are both fully perfected; seeing even the slightest fault, one gives rise to great dread; because the precepts are thus moistened, the food of the Dharma is fully satiated, and the mats of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are likewise thick.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The four dhyānas serve as the bed, and pure livelihood serves as the mattress.
Pure livelihood refers to the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising from non-attachment; therefore, non-attachment is taken as the bedding.
It is because it is beneath the bedding and upon the bed.
The pronunciation of "jiàn" (薦) is *qiàn* (見反); it is also a mat.
According to the *Yùpiān*, it is "the grass upon which beasts feed."
Furthermore, the "bedding" (chuáng) refers to that which is used for common reclining and support.
The character "xí" (廗) is pronounced xiáshí; according to the *Yùpiān*, "xí" (蓆) is pronounced qiángyì, meaning "broad and abundant."
The *Qieyun* dictionary lists it as "xí.
It is a metaphorical designation for father and son; furthermore, it uses soft language as if saying, "like my own son.
The character "ruò" (若) means "like"; that is, like my true son who has entered the holy path.
This refers to the period prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the passage from the *Sūtra*: "The householder was wise up to the point of managing the household affairs," the commentary states:
The fourth stage thus constitutes the rank of an Arya.
In the text, there is only mention of those beyond training (aśaikṣa); this gradually leads them into and out of [the path], while also manifesting the cultivation of the path (bhāvanāmārga).
Being made to remove refuse for twenty years is called "attending to household affairs."

From this point onward, they mutually trust one another in their mental states, and their coming and going encounter no difficulty; yet, as they still abide in their original place, their manifestation within the Path of Vision is termed "the Child."
Because the text is abbreviated.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, "He showed him gold and silver, [saying] 'I have no such things,'" the commentary says:
This illustrates the parable of not aspiring to greatness.
Although the two benefits of the Mahāyāna are made known, this is termed "entering and exiting.
The phrase "still outside the gate" means that the gates of the causes for Mahāyāna teaching and practice are outside.
"Taking up residence in a thatched hut" refers to dwelling in the stage of the Two Vehicles.
The character for "hut" (菴) is pronounced with the initial *wu* and the final *han* (烏含反);
it is a small grass shelter. Some write it as "菴" (ān), which refers to the ānlǚ grass and is not a shelter.
He thought to himself, "I have made poverty my livelihood; I am entirely without a share in the work of the Mahāyāna, nor do I harbor even a single aspiration to seek it.
This corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra: "The father knew his son's mind... down to the point where he became a kṣatriya householder."
The commentary states:
The second major section below consists of seven verses, which clarify what has now been attained.
Within the preceding analogy, there are two parts:
The first five verses concern the father’s entrustment to his son, while the latter two verses concern the son’s attainment [of the inheritance].
Within the former section, there are again two parts:
the first one and a half verses concern knowing the opportunity and assembling the kin, while the subsequent three and a half verses concern the formal entrustment of the family affairs.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "In this great assembly... to "...let them use it as they please," the commentary says:
The following three and a half verses properly entrust the household affairs.
There are five parts:
the first half-verse first instructs on generating the resolve (*bodhicitta*).
The first half-verse refers to his retreating from the flow of birth and death;

the second half-verse refers to his transformation of beings through the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*). This may have occurred when their faculties were ripening in the realms of humans or devas, or during the two paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), or at the two stages of severing the five lower and five upper fetters (*saṃyojana*). Therefore, it is said that he has seen his son for twenty years.
Some say that there are the fruits of those still training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
One verse concerns the former’s regression from the Mahāyāna and their subsequent meeting [with the Buddha] because their faculties have matured.
One verse concerns the formal entrustment.
The Sūtra says: "The son thought back to his former poverty until he attained what he had never before experienced.
The commentary states:
"The son has obtained it."
Conditioned merits are called "precious treasures.
Unconditioned *tathatā*, compassion, the mind, and so forth, are called "dwellings.

Furthermore, when consciousness realizes its fundamental nature and becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), it also knows that all sentient beings within the three realms have already obtained dwellings and acquired precious wealth; therefore, it gives rise to joy.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “The Buddha is also like this” up to “his śrāvaka disciples,” the commentary states:
The third major section below consists of thirty and a half verses, which together provide the explanation.
This section is divided into two parts:
the first twenty and a half verses praise the lack of aspiration for union in the past, while the subsequent ten verses praise the attainment of union in the present.
Within the first part, there are five prose sections; within the second part, there is the vision of the Buddha.
In this present verse, only the greatness [of the Buddha] and the lack of aspiration for union are explicitly shown; the remainder is omitted.
In the preceding prose section, there were three points showing greatness and the lack of aspiration; here it is likewise:

the first two verses correspond to the first point, wherein knowing that the Buddha does not say he has attained what they desire because they delight in the Lesser Vehicle, they have no aspiration for it.
Next, there are eight verses praising the third [ground], which are spoken solely for the sake of bodhisattvas and not for my own sake; therefore, I do not aspire for them.
The subsequent ten and a half verses praise the second [ground]; because one considers oneself to have attained nirvāṇa and believes one’s task is fulfilled, one does not aspire for it.
This was the first [instance].

He had never said, "You shall become Buddhas," nor that "I too have a share in the wondrous wisdom of a Buddha"; he merely said that we had attained the various outflows-free states as disciples of the Śrāvakas. Therefore, I did not aspire [to Buddhahood].
Regarding the sūtra passage, "The Buddha has commanded us that we shall surely attain Buddhahood," the commentary states:
The following eight verses praise the third [point], but they are spoken solely for the sake of the bodhisattvas and not correctly for my own sake; therefore, I do not aspire [to them].

The middle section is divided into six parts: first, one verse on the Buddha’s injunction; second, one and a half verses on my reliance upon the Buddha’s teaching; third, one verse on others relying upon my words; fourth, one verse on the Buddha bestowing predictions upon others; fifth, one and a half verses specifically for the sake of bodhisattvas and not for my own sake; and finally, two verses that conclude both through dharma and analogy.
This is the first instance.
The Buddha bestowed his empowerment through the three karmas and issued a secret injunction to preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras.
As the sūtra states: "I, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, have come to preach the Unsurpassed Way."
The commentary states:
These two types of selfhood rely upon the Buddha’s teachings.
As the sutra says: "O Sons of the Buddha, you should reach the stage of diligent cultivation."
The commentary states:
"The three types of 'self' based on others.
This refers to the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time, all Buddhas... up to "...shall attain Buddhahood."
The commentary states:
Regarding the four Buddhas bestowing predictions upon others, the term "all Buddhas" indicates that all Buddha-dharmas are identical; thus, it does not refer to a single Buddha alone.
Furthermore, because they were previously transformed by other Buddhas in the past, it could not be otherwise; for how could a single Buddha speak of "all" [Buddhas]?
Therefore, it was stated previously that they "had heard the teachings on skillful means from all Buddhas."
The Sūtra says: "All Buddhas have come to proclaim this essential truth.
The commentary states:
Because these five correct practices are for Bodhisattvas and not for my sake, I do not desire them.
The Sūtra says: "Just as it was with that impoverished son, so it is here.
The commentary states:
This concludes both the Dharma teaching and the analogy.
The meaning of the text is clear.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "We [attain] internal cessation" to "we do not take delight in anything at all," the commentary states:

The third section below consists of ten and a half verses. The second [section] concerns attaining nirvāṇa for oneself; because one has already reached fulfillment, there is no longing [for further attainment].
This is divided into two parts:
the first two verses state the fulfillment and lack of longing, while the subsequent eight and a half verses provide the explanation.
This is the first [type].

Regarding "internal cessation," it refers to the extinction of all afflictions within one's own person and the realization of nirvana; because they can only understand this as the ultimate goal and have no further external activities for the benefit of others, they do not aspire to the Great [Vehicle].
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “For what reason? up to “is called ultimate,” the commentary states:
the following eight and a half verses provide the explanation.
The middle section is divided into three parts:

the first three and a half verses concern the failure to aspire [for further attainment] because one considers oneself satisfied with having given rise to the contemplations of the three gates of liberation regarding the Buddha’s sphere and wisdom;
the next four verses concern the failure to aspire for oneself despite teaching others, because one considers that one has already repaid the Buddha’s kindness by attaining the Path.
The final verse concludes that he does not aspire [to Buddhahood] because the Buddha did not preach [the path for him];
this is the first [of the two parts].
The first three verses concern the contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*); the final one and a half verses concern the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
"All phenomena are empty" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Since the two types of self (*ātman*) do not exist, how could there be birth and so forth?
Next, the text below explains the six kinds of non-existents, such as arising and ceasing, which constitute the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*).
Having abandoned attachment and being without craving for anything, they consequently do not even seek after the Buddha’s wisdom; this is the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Having heard the profound intent of the *Prajñāpāramitā* regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they mistakenly interpret these as these three contemplations and believe they have attained nirvāṇa on their own. Later, taking this understanding to be the ultimate, they no longer aspire to the Great [Vehicle].
Regarding the sūtra passage, “We have, throughout the long night, repaid the Buddha’s kindness,” the commentary states:

These two verses, consisting of four lines, express that they have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness by attaining the Way; thus, although they speak for the sake of others, they themselves harbor no expectations.
This section is divided into two parts:
the first two and a half verses concern repaying the Buddha’s kindness, while the subsequent one and a half verses concern not seeking [recompense] for oneself despite speaking for others.
This is the former.

Examining the meaning of this passage, it indicates that they abide in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), rather than abiding in the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
As the Sūtra states: "Although we have reached a state where there is no longer any longing or desire for [further existence]..."
The commentary states:
Although he speaks for the sake of others, he himself has no expectations.
As the Sūtra says: "The Guide abandons him... down to 'there is a real benefit.'"
The commentary states:
"Because the three Buddhas did not speak for my sake, I have no desire [for their teaching].

Having discerned me, they perceived that my faculties were not yet mature and thus saw fit to abandon me; they never exhorted me to practice the Mahāyāna or spoke of its actual benefits, therefore I have no desire."
The initial phrase "did not exhort" refers to this present life; it does not mean he never exhorted them in the past, for he had already exhorted them long ago.
As the sutra says: "Like a wealthy elder who, upon arrival, then instructs [them] in great wisdom."
The commentary states:
The first twenty and a half verses correspond to what was previously not sought;
the following ten verses correspond to what is now attained. Regarding this latter point, there are two aspects:
The first three verses clarify the teaching through the correspondence of dharma and metaphor: the first teaches the provisional means, while the latter speaks of the ultimate truth;
the subsequent seven verses clarify that "I have now attained.
This is the first [of those seven].
One and a half verses are a metaphor, and one and a half verses are the teaching.
Regarding the sutra passage, "Today we have attained immeasurable treasure," the commentary says:
The seven verses below clarify what has now been attained.
This section is divided into three parts:

first, one and a half verses generally explain that what is now attained was not previously anticipated; next, three verses show that it is only from this day forward that it is called the essence of the fruit; finally, two and a half verses show that it is only from this point on that it is called the function of the fruit.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the Sūtra passage, “World-Honored One, I have now attained the unsurpassed,
supreme fruit,” the commentary says:
The second [verse] states that it is only from today onward that one is said to have attained the essence of the fruit.
The first verse generally distinguishes that the previously attained fruits were not real, whereas the present attainment is the reality.
"Path" (mārga) refers to realized wisdom; "fruit" (phala) refers to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Regarding the latter two verses, the attainment of the fruit is now the reality.

Based on the preceding causes, it is proven therein that the first verse concerns obtaining retribution through the cause of upholding the precepts, while the latter verse concerns attaining the great fruit through the perfection of the holy life (*brahmacarya*); both surpass those of the past.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "We who have now arrived should receive offerings," the commentary states:
"The three directions are termed the function of attaining the fruit."
The first verse attains the title of a "true śrāvaka" because of their benefit for others;
the latter one and a half verses attain the designation of a "true arhat" because they are a true field of merit.
This demonstrates that those who abide in the Lesser Vehicle are not true śrāvakas, nor are they truly arhats.
As the Sūtra says: "The Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One—whom is it possible to repay?"
The commentary states:
The seventy-three and a half verses above correspond to the preceding prose section.
From here on, the third segment of this chapter contains thirteen verses concerning the profound depth of the Buddha’s grace.
This is divided into two parts:

first, six and a half verses that generally clarify how profound the kindness is and how difficult it is to repay; second, six and a half verses that specifically clarify the matters that are difficult to repay.
Within the first part, there are further two sections:

The first one and a half verses clarify that because the Buddha’s compassion is profound, it is difficult to repay; the subsequent five verses clarify that although one performs acts of offering, one cannot repay [his kindness].
This is the first [of those five].

At that time, he traveled for a long distance over vast terrain with a mind full of diligence; he exhausted himself to benefit others with such profound sincerity that it was difficult to repay. The grace of the Great Heaven lies precisely in this.
As the Sūtra says: "He served him with his hands and feet, up to the point of honoring him with all his heart."
The commentary states:
The following five verses clarify the matter of making offerings.
This section is divided into two parts:

The first two verses state that the six kinds of internal wealth cannot repay [the Buddha's kindness]; the latter three verses state that the four kinds of external wealth, as well as the construction of stupas, likewise cannot repay it.
This is the first [point].
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, even with exquisite food, one still cannot repay [the debt].
The commentary states:
External objects, such as the four requisites, cannot repay it.
Two verses describe four matters, and one verse concludes them.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “The rareness of all Buddhas” to “teaching according to what is appropriate,” the commentary says:
The following six and a half verses clarify the matters that are difficult to repay.
Within this section, there are three parts:
the first two and a half verses generally clarify that the Buddha is able to perform inferior deeds for the sake of ordinary beings who grasp at signs, teaching them according to their needs.
The next two verses concern teaching the Dharma by knowing [the disciples'] desires, inclinations, and resolute convictions;
the final two verses concern teaching the three vehicles by knowing whether their faculties are mature or immature.
This is the first [of those].

To conceal the true virtues of the Sambhogakāya and manifest the provisional forms of the Nirmāṇakāya; to hide the profound essence of the wondrous principle and propagate the superficial teachings of coarse meaning; to not dwell in the Pure Land but instead reside in this defiled realm to follow after ordinary beings—how could this not be difficult to repay?
The Sūtra states: "The Buddhas, having arrived at the Dharma, preach the Dharma for them.
The commentary says:
This refers to the second [of the three ways], preaching the Dharma by knowing their desires, inclinations, and resolute convictions.

As for "resolute power," because it is rooted in profound conviction (*adhimukti*), one does not expound upon the profound and subtle according to one's own whims; rather, one accords with the inclinations of others by proclaiming these skillful means (*upāya*). How could this not be something difficult to repay?
Regarding the sūtra passage from "according to all sentient beings" up to "teaching according to what is appropriate," the commentary states:
These three [knowers] can discern whether the faculties [of sentient beings] are mature or immature, and thereby teach the three vehicles accordingly.

Whether coarse or subtle, real or provisional, he observes the faculties of beings from beginning to end and acts with skillful means; is this not a debt of profound gratitude that is difficult to repay?
The "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter is analyzed through three sections:
first, the purpose of its inclusion; second, the explanation of its title; and third, the resolution of objections.
There are four reasons for [the Buddha’s] coming:

first, previously, for those of superior faculties, he expounded the Dharma during the first cycle; Śāriputra received the Dharma through his realization, and the Buddha confirmed it, only afterwards granting him a prediction of enlightenment.

Now, as the second cycle has already provided an illustrative teaching for those of medium capacity, with four people serving as metaphors for its reception, the Buddha now returns to corroborate this through further illustration before finally bestowing the prediction; thus, this chapter follows.

Second, among the seven types of pride discussed in the treatises as objects of antidote, the third is the exclusive overweening pride (*abhimāna*) of Mahāyāna practitioners, who claim that there are no separate vehicles for Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
To counteract this, two parables are taught: the preceding "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta) serves to counteract ordinary beings who seek the sublime fruits of the human and celestial realms;

the subsequent "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (Adhimukti-parivarta) serves to counteract those of the Two Vehicles who, while still in training, cling to their own vehicles as equal to the Tathāgata’s vehicle and thus fail to seek the Buddha-vehicle.

This present chapter serves as an antidote to the one-sided arrogance of those who follow the Mahāyāna, who claim that there is no distinction between the two vehicles and that there is only the One Vehicle.

Therefore, that treatise states: "The third person is intended to make known the differences among the various vehicles; the Tathāgatas teach the Dharma with impartiality, for the sprouts [of enlightenment] grow according to the seeds of the roots of goodness of sentient beings."
This signifies that although the single rain is the same, the growth of the three types of grass and two types of trees differs;

likewise, although the Buddha’s teaching is the same, the cultivation undertaken by those of the three vehicles and two types of noble ones is distinct. This is because the capacities of sentient beings are each different, and because there are those who are definitively fixed in the two vehicles, due to the differences in their innate dispositions and the resulting variations in how they receive the moisture of the Dharma.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"A son of good family who upholds the True Dharma is capable of bearing the four burdens. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also says:

"At one time I taught the One Vehicle and the Single Path; yet my disciples, failing to understand my intention, claimed that those such as the *srotāpanna* all attain the Buddha-way," as is explained at length elsewhere.
A vehicle (*yāna*) is so named because it carries people; thus, the teachings and so forth are called vehicles.
Although the Buddha-dharma is the same, there are differences in the capacities and practices of sentient beings; therefore, this chapter is taught.

Thirdly, at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛiccheda*), both wisdom and the gateways [to liberation] were designated as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) because both are profoundly deep.

The preceding "Parable Chapter" states that while there are three vehicles, their essence is but one; the four types of people understand this reality of one and the provisional designation of three, thereby realizing the profundity of wisdom.

This present "gate of the assembly" (samāja-mukha) refers to the Āgamas; while the teaching is the same, the capacities of the practitioners differ, hence it is called the "assembly" that brings them together at this gate.

For example, when the Four Noble Truths are taught, those with the three faculties hear them all together; yet, depending on the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), elements (dhātus), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the three natures (trisvabhāva), there are differences in their cultivation, which are termed the "Three Vehicles" (triyāna).
Therefore, we know that while the teaching is the same, the capacities [of the recipients] differ; hence this chapter follows.
Fourth, among the ten unsurpassed qualities, it is said: "The first is to manifest the unsurpassed nature of the seeds; therefore, the analogy of rain is taught."
The ten unsurpassed [qualities] are all comprised within the seven similes, with the three equalities as the remainder.
Among these, there are cases where the remainder pertains to the text and cases where the remainder pertains to the meaning; this instance is a remainder of meaning, not a remainder of text.
Among the seven similes, there is already the simile of rain; it is stated once more within the ten unsurpassed [teachings] and is thus termed "residual.

The previous exposition of the rain simile spoke of the universal moistening of the three types of grass; since these three types of grass are distinct, it serves to make known the differences among the vehicles (*yāna*).

Now, regarding the rain metaphor, among the three types of grass that are moistened, two types of grass are compared in form: the "Buddha-seed" is called the great grass; when its own stage is compared with others, they are further designated as the two trees. Because the meanings of what is intended are distinct, they are termed "residual meanings."

Alternatively, this may be due to a textual corruption, referring to the small, medium, and large cursive scripts; the text concerns the analogy of rain to refute the common fallacy regarding the vehicles, wherein various trees—small, medium, and large—each receive [the rain] according to their superior, middling, or inferior capacities.
This metaphor of rain represents the unsurpassed nature of the seed; because the preceding and following passages differ in context, this is a fragmentary text.
When these great seeds receive the nourishment of rain, their essence and function become vast and expansive, and because they subsequently yield extraordinary fruits, they are called "unsurpassed."
The treatise cites a sūtra which says: "That which is not separate from my own body is the unsurpassed meaning; it exists only in the Mahāyāna, for it is called 'not separate.
Whether as seeds or as manifestations, whether as causes or as fruits, all are indeed not separate from the Mahāyāna."
Now, it is revealed that the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of the Mahāyāna serve as the causal basis for the attainment of the Buddha-body.
This chapter has been composed in order to demonstrate the supremacy of these seeds.
Regarding the explanation of names: that which dispels illness through its divine power is called "medicine" (yào); that which receives moisture and nourishment in form is called "grass" (cǎo).
There are things that are medicine but not grass, things that are grass but not medicine, things that are both grass and medicine, and things that are neither grass nor medicine;
the metaphors employed here are likewise so.
The teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit are all termed "medicine.
Here, we take the medicine of practice—receiving the teaching and cultivating it to give rise [to realization]—and do not take other medicinal stones, for they cannot cause growth.

All seeds capable of growth, whether mundane or supramundane, are collectively termed "grass. Here, however, we take the seeds of goodness of humans and devas, as well as the causal wisdom of the Three Vehicles, to be the medicinal grasses because they counteract and harm evil;
we do not take the seeds of the evil paths of birth and death, for they grow by not receiving the True Dharma.

The intention here is to distinguish the specific categories of the three vehicles, wherein those who receive the teaching establish their respective distinct vehicles; it does not seek to provide a universal illumination of all categories. Therefore, "medicinal herbs" is used as the title.
These are medicines that are also grasses; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
By distinguishing the specific from the general, "medicinal herb" (*oṣadhi-tṛṇa*) is interpreted according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Using this as a metaphor, it is called the "Medicinal Herb Simile.

If one were to say that this chapter is named the "Medicinal Herb Simile" because it explains both the simile of medicine and the simile of herbs—rather than meaning that the medicine itself is the herb—then would all grasses be intended as the subject of the metaphor?
For this reason, it is known that what is now being taught is correct.
This employs two meanings as metaphors:
first, just as the natures of grasses differ, so they receive rain and their respective types flourish; [the second is as follows:]...
Third, because their fundamental capacities differ, they receive the teachings and thereby form the three vehicles.
Second, just as grasses possess natures that do not know one another;

third, the faculties are likewise unable to know the differences between the five types of vehicles, for it is said that there is no distinction among the vehicles. Therefore, the medicinal herbs are used as a metaphor.
Regarding the resolution of objections:

Question—In the treatise, the explanations of the seven similes and the ten unsurpassed qualities all refer to the "simile of rain. For what reason is the title of this chapter given as the "Simile of the Medicinal Herbs" rather than the "Simile of Rain Chapter"?
Answer:
The treatise explains the phenomena that nourish [the earth] in order to manifest the metaphor; therefore, it uses "rain" as the name of the metaphor.
The sutra takes the substance of the metaphor to dispel those doubts; therefore, it designates "medicinal herbs."

Those who hold inverted views take the lack of distinction among vehicles as their affliction, while those who engage in refutation take the distinction among capacities as their basis for refutation. Therefore, the medicinal herbs moistened by the rain are used as a metaphor for the root-natures nourished [by the teaching]; for this reason, the rain itself is not designated as the primary analogy, nor are both the rain and the herbs presented together as the subject of the chapter.
Question:
This chapter also mentions "two pieces of wood"; why then is it not titled the "Chapter on Grasses and Trees"?
Answer:

To speak according to the facts, both [the grasses and the trees] should have been cited together; however, since the establishment of the True Dharma was fundamentally intended to cure the disease of birth, and because birth possesses the ailment of "concordant progression," it was cured by means of the diversity of grasses.

The Unsurpassed [Vehicle] reveals the sublime and exalted essence, which does not yet involve curing the disease of birth; therefore, this chapter is titled after the medicinal herbs, rather than being designated by the name of the trees and so forth.

The grass is broad while the wood is narrow; the grass is small while the wood is large. This demonstrates that [the rain] penetrates all three vehicles and is not limited to the Great Vehicle alone; it demonstrates that its moistening and growth-fostering power is not limited to mere maturation.
Therefore, some explain it thus: "Medicine" refers to the rain, for the medicine of the Dharma can nourish;
"grass" refers to the spiritual capacity (*indriya*), which is the nature that is nurtured and produced.
Using medicine as a metaphor for the Dharma and grass as a metaphor for the capacities [of sentient beings], once both are clearly manifested, there is no longer any difficulty.
Although the text does not state it so, how could the underlying principle be at fault?

Furthermore, in the previous "Simile Chapter," there was the burning house to be loathed and the three vehicles to be delighted in; these two combined similes could only be discussed in general terms.
Here, because the capacities to be moistened differ and one must remedy the malady of clinging to a single [vehicle], only the medicinal herbs are used as a metaphor.
The Sūtra says, "At that time, the World-Honored One... [up to] 'could not be fully described.
The Commentary states:
Within this chapter, the main text is divided into three sections:

First, there is the praise of the seal; next, from "Kāśyapa, you should know" onwards, is the formal exposition; finally, at the end of the chapter, the two verses conclude that the teaching of reality constitutes the gradual process of bestowing the prediction of enlightenment.
This is the first [section].
First, there is praise for the seal (*mudrā*); subsequently, there is further expression of wonder.
It is called "well done" (*sādhu*) because the words accord with reason; it is called a "seal" because its meaning accords with reality.
This demonstrates that what he said has not yet exhausted the Buddha’s virtues; therefore, he further praises the Buddha by likening him to the elder, using the small to illustrate the great.
Since you, like the impoverished son, possess only a slight share of the Sage’s virtue, he likewise permits this comparison; thus, he offers praise and provides his seal of approval.
"Sincerity" (*cheng*) means faithfulness and reverence;
for faithfulness is acting as one speaks, and reverence is speaking as one acts.
The virtues of the Buddha are inconceivable, and it is impossible to exhaustively describe them.
The Sūtra says: “Kāśyapa, you should know... up to ... it is not in vain.
The commentary states:
The following provides a detailed exposition.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the prose section; second, the verse section.
The first part contains two sub-sections:

First is the exposition, second is the conclusion regarding what is about to follow; this begins from the verse: "The Tathāgata knows that this is of one characteristic and one flavor," and continues below.
Within the first [section], there are three parts:
first, the exposition by means of the Dharma; second, the exposition by means of a simile; third, the exposition by means of application.
Within the Dharma there are four points:

first, the Buddha’s appearance in the world; second, the Dharma benefiting all sentient beings; third, the differences among those who receive the Way; and fourth, the inability to attain realization on one's own.
This is the first.
Possessing mastery over all phenomena, his teachings are never in vain; thus he appears in the world to guide and benefit all sentient beings.
As the Sūtra says: "Regarding all phenomena, he has reached the stage of omniscience."
The commentary states:
These two dharmas benefit all sentient beings.
Through great compassionate wisdom and skillful means, they are able to skillfully expound upon dharmas that are free from names and characteristics, thereby benefiting all sentient beings.
The principle thus explained also accords with the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom, for it is taught in accordance with realization.

"Arriving" (dào) carries the meaning of reaching accord; whether it be the teaching conforming to the principle, the principle conforming to practice, or practice conforming to the fruit, it is therefore said that one arrives at the stage of the Buddha-fruit, thereby universally nourishing those who are to be transformed.
The Sūtra states: “The Tathāgata observes and knows, up to attaining unimpeded penetration.
The commentary says:
There are distinctions among the three types of paths of feeling.

Because it is the ultimate true nature to which consciousness returns—the emptiness of phenomena—and because it knows the inclinations and movements of the minds of sentient beings, it is able to cause each of them to grow and develop accordingly.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "There is that which has no destination, yet it is the intended object of aspiration. Therefore, the destination to which one returns is precisely the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); because it is the ultimate destination, it is suchness (*tathatā*). That which the mind pursues is the practice of universal aspiration (*sarvatraga-caryā*) toward what is cherished.

One attains unimpeded mastery within the wisdom of principle (jñāna) and phenomena (dharma), or because the Buddha understands the dharmas and the mental activities of sentient beings, he is able to receive them into the Path and distinguish the three vehicles.
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, up to all-encompassing wisdom."
The commentary states:
These four [categories] cannot realize [the truth] on their own.

The Buddha is able to exhaustively master all phenomena; therefore, he can discern the capacities and natures of beings, first providing the three vehicles and later revealing to sentient beings the wisdom of the Buddha.
Sentient beings are not like this; by what principle could they know their own nature or the nature of others?
Both the following analogies and their applications possess this potential, which is why they are divided into four sections.
Furthermore, another explanation states that there are two ways of describing phenomena (*dharma*): [the description of the phenomenon itself and the description of its characteristics].

First, there is a general explanation that what is spoken by the One Who Attains Sovereignty over Dharmas (*dharmeśvara*) is not in vain; second, from "With wisdom and skillful means regarding all dharmas" onwards, there is a specific manifestation of its non-falsity.
Within this specific manifestation of non-falsity, there are four parts:
first, the ability to open up the two entities of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, thereby enlightening the minds of sentient beings; "expounding with wisdom and skillful means," and so forth, refers to this.
Second, it can manifest *tathatā* to demonstrate it to sentient beings; this is "the destination to which all dharmas return.
Third, because it can awaken one to the wisdom of *bodhi*, it is "awakening sentient beings so that they attain unimpeded penetration.
Fourth, because it has personally entered [this state] and enables others to enter as well, it is "demonstrating all-encompassing wisdom."
Although this interpretation is made, if one follows the perspective of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), the subsequent passage actually constitutes a distinct meaning.
Furthermore, there is a separate manifestation of the fourfold non-falsity:

first, exhausting the true nature of phenomena; second, being able to know emptiness and existence; third, knowing the joy of the arising mind; and fourth, being able to demonstrate the provisional and the real.
Regarding the phrase "by means of wisdom and skillful means" and so forth: although the Dharma is in reality beyond words, its elucidation through speech is termed "wisdom and skillful means.
Although the Dharma taught by this wisdom and skillful means is not itself the ultimate truth, it is nonetheless no different from the Dharma realized by the Buddha’s wisdom.
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) means a basis; it is the locus upon which the Buddha’s wisdom observes, and the true realm is called "ground.

This refers to the Buddha’s teaching on the principles of ultimate and conventional truth (*satya*), which, being in perfect accord with the sphere of the Buddha’s wisdom, are non-different in essence and conform to the actual phenomena (*dharmas*).

Alternatively, the teaching can accord with principle, principle can accord with practice, and practice can accord with the fruit; thus one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, for all-knowing wisdom is the wisdom of a Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata observes and knows" and so forth: this refers to the knowledge of the ultimate destination of all phenomena—both empty and existent—which are the three natures of phenomena: the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva), and the perfected (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Alternatively, that which is the destination is the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), for it is the ultimate place of resort for all phenomena.

"Also knowing the deep-seated mental activities of sentient beings" means knowing their mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) as well as what their deep-seated minds delight in practicing; that is, to penetrate the minds of sentient beings and their pervasive courses of action without obstruction.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, with respect to all dharmas," etc.: having attained ultimate and clear understanding of all dharmas, one is thus able to manifest wisdom for sentient beings, employing the three provisional means and the one reality to inspire them toward joyful realization.

The underlying intention here is as follows: the dharmas of consciousness and the emptiness of intrinsic nature within the realm of the wisdom that accords with the teachings have been explained; by understanding the path to be practiced through the activities of the mind, one is able to manifest the Buddha’s wisdom to sentient beings and cause them to enter it.
Because of these four meanings, what is taught is not in vain; because what is taught is not in vain, the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless.
How could you possibly explain it?

The Buddha knows all phenomena and discerns the minds of sentient beings; therefore, he first employs skillful means and subsequently teaches the true Dharma, whereby sentient beings who receive it achieve the distinctions of the five vehicles.

Sentient beings lack such merit and wisdom; they do not recognize the essence of dharmas nor the minds of sentient beings. How, then, could they know the provisional and the ultimate aspects of dharmas, yet cling to the notion that the three vehicles have no difference?
The Sūtra says: “Kāśyapa, it is like [the case where] name and form are each distinct.
The commentary states:
This is the explanation by way of analogy.
The middle section is divided into two parts:
first, the general analogy; second, the specific analogies.
This is the first part.
The preceding section used "land" as a metaphor for that which is capable of producing; the following section uses it as a metaphor for that which is produced.
"The trichiliocosm" characterizes the vessel-world upon which [beings] rely; it is the realm of transformation of a single Buddha.
Among these, there are four [categories];
the first is "mountain. The *Yupian* states: "Gen is the mountain; 'shan' means to produce. It proclaims the vital energy and disperses it so that the myriad things are born."
The two *chuān* (rivers) flow through and penetrate each other;
they are water. The three *xī* (gullies): according to the *Erya*, "water that flows into a *chuān* is called a *xī*.
The four *gǔ* (valleys): pronounced *gǔ* (as in "ancient") or, according to the *Yùpiān*, also *yúyù*; water that flows into a *xī* is called a *gǔ*.
The *Shuowen* states: "A valley (*gu*) is a stream through which a spring flows.
This serves as a metaphor for the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) within the great trichiliocosm.
Among all that exists within these lands, "herbs" (*hui*) refer to the three types of grasses, and "trees" (*mu*) refer to the two types of trees.
The character "huì" (卉) has the phonetic value of *xǔ guì* (許貴反); it is a general term for all hundred grasses and also signifies "multitude.
Both grasses (*huì*) and trees (*mù*) have "thickets" (*cóng*) and "forests" (*lín*), which serves to clarify that both plants and trees each exist in great numbers.
Although these are numerous, among them the seeds of mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas are likened to medicinal herbs.
The essential natures of the seeds of the five vehicles are distinct, like various species; their characteristics and functions differ, like the divergence between names and forms.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to both physical appearance and the category of material phenomena.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "Dense clouds spread everywhere throughout the great trichiliocosm," the commentary states:
The following provides specific analogies, which are fourfold:

first, the analogy of the Dharma King appearing in the world; second, the analogy of the teaching being universally nourished; third, the analogy of receiving moisture differently according to individual capacity; and fourth, the analogy of lacking self-awareness.
“Dense clouds spread everywhere” is the first metaphor.
“Pervadingly covering” and what follows is the second metaphor.

The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) conceals the reality body (dharmakāya), gradually manifesting the eight phases [of a Buddha’s life] to secretly and extensively benefit beings; this is like clouds that are dense and widespread, rather than sudden, violent storms, for they do not cause calamity.
Clouds possess ten virtues, which are explained in the verses themselves.

First, when the transformation-buddhas manifest simultaneously throughout the three thousandfold world-system, their voices likewise pervade it; therefore, it is said that they "pervade and fill the great trichiliocosm."
Regarding the passage from "At one time [the rain] poured down equally" to "and all the medicinal herbs," the commentary states:
This is the third section below, the analogy of how those who receive the moisture differ.
There are two [parts]:
the first is nourished by rain, while the latter receives moisture in various ways.
The first section consists of three parts:
First is the general heading; second is horizontal proliferation; third is vertical growth.
This is the first.
"At one time" means that the capacities of the audience had matured.
“Equally showering” (*dengshu*) means that when a single sound is expounded, each person understands it according to their own capacity.
The character for “shower” (*shu*) is pronounced as *shù* or *shí yù* (the latter meaning seasonal rain).
Now, returning to the beginning:
its moisture is universally pervasive, for its benefits nourish all equally.
"Qiá" (洽) is pronounced with the initial *h* and final *-jiao*; it means to moisten and to permeate everywhere, carrying the sense of harmonizing and sprinkling throughout.
The "herbs, trees, forests, and thickets" are explained as before.
"Medicinal herbs" are a metaphor for the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The Sūtra says: "From small roots and small stems to large branches and large leaves."
The commentary states:
This is an excessive proliferation.

Since the natures of the three vehicles differ, the fault of [erroneously] asserting that the vehicles are identical is refuted; because there are three types of root-nature, they are divided into three kinds.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"For example, there are three kinds of patients: first, those who will certainly recover whether they encounter a skilled physician or not"—this refers to the great grasses.
"Second, if one encounters [the remedy], one recovers; if one does not encounter it, one does not recover"—this refers to the grasses herein.
"Third, whether one encounters it or not, one definitely cannot recover"—this refers to the small grasses herein.

Within each of these three vehicles, there arise "elders" consisting of four factors—teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—therefore it is said that each possesses roots, stems, branches, and leaves.

This is because one realizes the principle by relying on the teaching, gives rise to practice by relying on the principle, and attains the fruit by relying on practice; thus they follow the sequential order of growth, such as that of roots, stems, and so forth.
Furthermore, these are assigned respectively according to the superior or inferior results, practices, principles, and teachings.
Moreover, it is explained that within each of these three, there are four factors: first, the spiritual lineage (*gotra*);
second, the arousal of the resolve (*cittotpāda*); third, the practice (*pratipatti*); and fourth, the attainment of the result (*phala-prāpti*).

These four correspond to the three [categories], being assigned to them respectively: they are called "horizontal" as the three vehicles (*yāna*), and "vertical" as the four types; they are termed horizontal because these types exist based on their respective natures (*gotra*).

There is also an explanation that the four are those of superior resolve (*adhimukti*), vision (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); however, this meaning is not universal, as it exists even among the small grasses, and thus it is not adopted here.
The Sūtra says: "From the various trees, large and small, each receives its respective [portion].
The Commentary states:
This refers to vertical height.
The treatise states that the great tree is not separate from my own body; this is the supreme meaning of the seed.

Among the great grasses, there are distinguished as small trees and great trees: prior to the stage of non-retrogression, they are called small trees; subsequent to the stage of non-retrogression, they are called great trees.
This has two meanings:

first, it is said that those prior to the seventh stage are called "small trees," while those from the eighth stage upward are called "great trees," because they possess the four kinds of non-retrogression.

According to the subsequent verse, one merely divides the two types of wood into inferior, intermediate, and superior; thus, the two woods are combined to distinguish three grades. Specifically, the five stages and below are termed "inferior," because one has newly attained the bliss of *samāpatti* and the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
The sixth, seventh, and eighth stages are "intermediate," because one attains the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
The ninth and tenth stages are "superior," because one attains the mind-made body of spontaneous action that is co-emergent with its kind (*jātisamutthāna-anabhisamskāra-manomaya-kāya*).
There is an interpretation that this is not so: what category does the stage prior to the first bhūmi belong to? Is it not the "small wood"?
If one follows this meaning, the stages prior to the first bhūmi are designated as "inferior" because they consist exclusively of impure cultivation;
the first seven bhūmis are designated as "middling" because they consist of a mixture of both impure and pure cultivation.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is called "superior," because it consists purely of untainted cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*).

Second, it is said that prior to the first stage it is called a "small tree," while from the first stage upward it is called a "great tree," because one has realized non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Each of the two trees, the small and the large, has its own lower, middle, and upper grades: the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute the three grades of the small tree; the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) are subsumed within the first abode, the abode of initial resolve; and the four roots of goodness of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are subsumed within the tenth dedication.

For this reason, the *Avataṃsaka* speaks only of thirty stages and does not speak of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), because within the stage of "Abiding in the Production of the Thought" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), the eight aspects [of enlightenment] are accomplished.
Furthermore, it does not speak of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), because within the "Infinite Dedication to the Dharma Realm," one abides in the four contemplations.

It is simply stated that Śāriputra’s cultivation of the path regressed after sixty kalpas; this means he had reached the completion of the sixth stage but had not yet entered the seventh stage of non-retrogression. Thus, we know that the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) have no separate status [beyond the stages], and for this reason, only thirty-three asaṃkhyeya kalpas are mentioned.
There are three stages prior to the bhūmis, for four are not mentioned.

The *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts state that one cultivates the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) once the first kalpa is completed; they do not mention a long duration because these are cultivated during a separate kalpa.
Therefore, the four roots of goodness are subsumed within the ten dedications.
Regarding the three stages of the great tree: the first, second, and third stages are termed "lower," as they are similar to the mundane;
the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are termed "middle," as they are only then similar to the supramundane.
The names "seven, eight, nine, and ten" are designated as "superior" because they transcend the worldly paths of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

If it is said that all three types of grasses possess inferior, middling, and superior qualities, then among the small grasses, humans are described as inferior, the desire-realm devas as middling, and the form-realm devas as superior.

Regarding the three grades of middling practitioners: those on the seven stages of expedient means are classified as lower; those who are noble learners (śaikṣa) are classified as middling; and those beyond learning (aśaikṣa) are called superior.
Whereas the preceding [classification] traversed the three vehicles horizontally, the present one penetrates the three stages vertically.
The Sūtra says: "From the rain showered by a single cloud... down to the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruits.
The commentary states:
"The moisture they receive varies according to each [plant]."
The capacity to nourish is one, yet the plants and trees so nourished each have their own distinctions.

"Growth" (sheng) is a metaphor for the initial aspiration; "maturation" (zhang) is a metaphor for subsequent practice; "the blooming of flowers" (huafu) is a metaphor for hearing the teachings and practicing them; and "the ripening of fruit" (guoshi) is a metaphor for realizing the principle and attaining the result.
The character "shu" (敷) is pronounced with the initial *fu* and the final *-fu*; it means to open or to display.

Because each [being] receives moisture according to their own nature, they grow flowers and fruits that differ from one another. When the teaching is applied to the principle while forgetting the specific capacity (*mātra*), or when the teaching is applied to later indeterminate natures and so forth to bring them to maturity, this is called "one rain" and also "one sound. This is because the principle of the Dharma taught is of a single characteristic, and those of regressive nature ultimately all become Buddhas.

When the teaching is adapted to the capacities of beings such that they forget the underlying principles and methods, or when it is employed for those at the initial stage whose faculties are not yet matured, this is called the "Three Vehicles" (triyāna) and is also termed the "Three Chariots."

According to their respective capacities, there are initially three types of Dharma teachings presented as side-guides; thus, the teachings that encompass these practices are called the "Three Piṭakas," for they expound the distinctions among the practices of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

If the teachings are categorized according to how they encompass the principles and how they are spoken in response to specific capacities, they are called the two piṭakas, namely the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
The *Ajaśatru-rāja-sūtra* also speaks of three piṭakas, namely the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka, and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

Now, when the teaching is contrasted with the principle and the subsequent capacities are unified, it is termed "a single cloud and rain. That which nourishes those three types of capacities according to their respective natures is called the "Three Vehicles.
Since the manifestation of the principle has corresponding capacities, it is clear that there are differences among the vehicles.

The names of the "Pitakas" (piṭaka) are established by taking the teachings as they respond to specific capacities and clarifying their meanings through principles; the designation of the "Vehicles" (yāna) is established by using the teachings that reveal these principles to transport sentient beings.
These are the two distinctions.
Regarding the sutra passage from "Although produced from the same ground" to "each has its own distinctions," the commentary says:
This is the fourth illustration below, concerning the lack of self-awareness.
The lineages of the three vehicles depend upon one true principle and arise from one ground; they rely upon one Buddha’s teaching and are moistened by one rain.
Just as various grasses and trees, though they receive moisture differently, do not themselves perceive this, nor do they know that others receive moisture and grow.
This interpretation seems somewhat superficial; one should seek to understand it thoroughly.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “Kāśyapa, you should know... up to ‘like a great cloud arising’,” the commentary says:
The third section below is a combined summary, also consisting of four parts, each of which has two sections: first, the presentation of the Dharma, followed by the metaphorical application.
This applies the analogy to the appearance of the Dharma King in the world.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "With a great voice" up to "throughout the great trichiliocosm," the commentary states:
This second section collectively explains that the teaching universally nourishes [all beings].
Not only does his body pervade [the assembly], but his voice likewise pervades it.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, "In the midst of the great assembly... up to the Buddha, the World-Honored One," the commentary says:
The third section below concerns the distinct ways in which they receive and benefit from the moisture;
it has two parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma, and second, the application through analogy.
The beginning has four parts:

first, the self-proclamation and summoning; second, others hearing it and arriving en masse; third, the Buddha responding to guide and benefit them; fourth, sentient beings hearing it and obtaining benefit.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
First, one proclaims for oneself; later, one summons others to assemble.
There are three types of proclamations:
first, the proclamation of virtuous titles; second, the proclamation of utility; and third, the proclamation of knowledge and vision.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sutra passage from "those not yet crossed over" to "causing them to attain nirvana," the commentary says:
This invocation is efficacious and can fulfill the four vows.
"Du" (to cross over) carries the meaning of transcending and surpassing.
"Resolution" (*vimukti*) means the sense of severing [afflictions] through cultivation.

First, for those who have not yet escaped suffering, one vows that they may escape suffering; second, for those who have not yet severed evil and cultivated goodness, one vows that they may sever evil and cultivate goodness; third, for those who have not yet attained peace and happiness, one vows that they may attain peace and happiness; fourth, for those who have not yet become Buddhas and attained *nirvāṇa*, one vows that they may become Buddhas and attain *nirvāṇa*.

The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states that "knowing suffering, severing its origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path constitute the four great vows"; this is precisely what is meant here.
Within these four, suffering, origin, the path, and cessation are to be assigned respectively.
Regarding the sūtra passage from "in this life and in future lives" up to "one who speaks the path," the commentary states:
This proclaims knowledge and vision.
There are three:
first, the proclamation of the Three Knowledges; second, the proclamation of the Two Wisdoms; and third, the proclamation of the Three Dharmas.
To know this life and future lives is the proclamation of the Three Knowledges.
That which has already been seen is called "present," because both the present and the past are [conceptually] present.
All-knowing is true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*); all-seeing is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Alternatively, the former refers to these two knowledges, while the latter refers to the five eyes.
"Knowing, opening, and explaining" means: knowing all objects, opening all practices, and explaining all fruits;
knowing the correct and the deviant, opening the wholesome and the unwholesome, and explaining cessation and cultivation.
Furthermore, one knows the Mahāyāna, the opening for pratyekabuddhas, and the teaching for śrāvakas;
as well as ordinary beings, those in training (śaikṣa), and those beyond training (aśaikṣa);

and the three groups of the wrong, the right, and the indeterminate; the three faculties, the three aggregates, the three times, the Three Jewels, the three poisons, the three virtues, the three realms, the three outflows, and so forth.
Furthermore, they discern birth and death, demonstrate the heterodox and the orthodox, and explain the open and the obstructed.
Moreover, they awaken to and know all paths, being able to provide concise expositions and detailed explanations.
These should be assigned accordingly.
There is one kind of path, namely the Single Vehicle (ekayāna) or the Single Path;
there are two kinds of paths: the wholesome and unwholesome realms, and the mundane and supramundane.
Up to the ten paths of action and so forth, all should be understood according to principle.
The Sūtra says: "You gods and humans, come for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
The commentary states:
The former was a proclamation; this is a summons.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "At that time, countless [beings]... came to listen to the Dharma," the commentary states:
The second [section] concerns the universal arrival of those who have heard [the teaching] from others.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the Tathāgata attained a most excellent benefit.
The commentary states:
This is the third [occasion] of the Buddha’s beneficial guidance.
For those of sharp faculties, he teaches the Mahāyāna; for those of dull faculties, he teaches the Two Vehicles.
